doc_summary: The paper argues that failure of existing NLP attacks on aligned LLMs is not evidence of robustness, and validates attack strength with known-solution test cases built by brute force; it then shows multimodal models are easily attacked via continuous image inputs. The methodological stance is that negative results need a calibrated, positive-control check before being believed.

items.claim: prefers validating an evaluation against test cases with known, constructed-by-brute-force positive answers over trusting a failed attack as evidence of robustness because a failure may just reflect a weak attack.
items.quote: first, we construct test cases with known adversarial examples that we have identified a priori; then, we run the attack on these test cases and verify they succeed.

items.claim: Distrusts the inference 'our attacks/evals did not find the behavior, therefore the model is safe', since absence of elicitation may reflect an insufficiently powerful probe.
items.quote: the failure of current attacks should not be seen as proof that aligned text models remain aligned under adversarial inputs.

items.claim: prefers evaluation tests where existence of a solution is guaranteed by construction over open-ended tests because then any failure unambiguously indicates a flawed tool.
items.quote: Observe that a sufficiently strong attack (e.g. a brute force search over all prompts) will always succeed on this test: any failure thus indicates a flawed attack.

items.claim: In a setup, respect the real deployment format (fixed chat template, attacker controls only the user turn, prior history unmodifiable) instead of giving the adversary unrealistic control over the prompt because unrealistic control makes the result irrelevant to real deployments.
items.quote: the attacker controls the tokens right before the model’s generation, which makes an attack much easier (but not relevant for current chat bot deployments).

items.claim: In a setup, build the context from real benign conversation data (Open Assistant truncated to random lengths) instead of hand-written prompts because it makes the surrounding context natural and varied.
items.quote: This dataset consists of a series of hypothetical interactions between a human and an assistant, which we truncate to a randomly selected $K\in[1..N]$ rounds.

items.claim: Inspects samples qualitatively to catch failures of the automated metric, and flags cheap metrics' limits instead of trusting them blindly.
items.quote: But in less than ten cases, we find our automated metric has potential limitations.

items.claim: prefers worst-case, existence-style evaluation of behavior over modeling a specific realistic adversary because it gives a lower bound on what models can be made to do.
items.quote: for the most part we are not concerned with any particular practical adversary, and instead, only with finding any valid input that achieves our attack goal.

items.claim: Chooses the tested behavior (toxicity) mainly because it is cheaply auto-evaluable, openly acknowledging a simplistic proxy.
items.quote: The main reason is that toxicity is relatively easy to (approximately) evaluate in a automated way.

items.claim: Tests on the easier model first so that failure there is informative about harder targets.
items.quote: as GPT-2 is an easier model to attack, if attacks fail here, they are unlikely to succeed on the more difficult cases of aligned models.

items.claim: States that future attacks should pass the proposed known-solution tests before being considered reliable, and that the goal is better defense evaluation.
items.quote: Such attacks should, at a minimum, pass our tests to be considered reliable.
